en: “My beloved two lions,
You are the lights of two lions.
You too were a khan's son;
Semetey, you too are a khan's only son.
Today, do not darken my blood,
Embracing and weeping,
Do not darken my soul.
My beloved two lions,
I have words to say to you.
I too am parted from my twins,
And have a grief that will not heal.
My pair of twin lambs too—
Parted from them both alike,
I too have lived unable to die.
I too wish to die from anguish;
I remain alive, not dying,
Because you two lions left by our lords
Are both still alive.”
The elder Bakai, a Kozhosan,
A saint who had seen much,
Who taught what was unknown,
The learned elder Bakai,
Who made the unperceived perceived,
The hawklike saint Bakai,
Stepped between them, and the two
The saint separated.
For the utterly naked child,
Seven black young bulls
He had slaughtered,
And made the child's votive offering as alms.
When they set out here from Bukhara,
That noble mother of yours, Kanykei,
The beauty of dusky complexion,
The most radiant among Muslims,
The youngest of twelve girls,
God's beloved servant,
My noble, fierce-tempered mother
Was a woman of sacred power.
On my mother's right shoulder,
Events six months ahead
He could tell at once:
Naked Kyzyr was there.
My noble mother Kanykei
Was just such a saintly soul.
My learned, saintly mother
Had entrusted a white saddlebag,
A saddlebag just right for her dear Semetey.
My noble, luckless mother
Tied it tightly once again,
And fastened it to the saddle straps,
Weeping in grief to the one God,
Dedicating it to her dear Kulchoro.
There are wonders still to tell:
Inside that saddlebag
Was a coat entrusted for Kulchoro.
This woman, weeping in Bukhara,
Had made a coat,
Dedicating it to Kulchoro.
That coat she had made
Had a golden collar and brazen sleeves,
Double mail with lark-eye rings,
An outer robe, a broad jacket.
The graceful woman Kanykei
Had provided it for the boy.
Its handsome clasps were gold;
Its price was very costly.
There was writing on its collar:
‘For orphan Kulchoro to wear,’
His name written with honor.
Acknowledging his orphanhood,
The charge his mother had given
They put upon Kulchoro.
Of white cloth with a silken weft,
The shirt she had sewn specially,
They put on underneath.
The noble woman Kanykei,
‘Let the cherished orphan wear them,’ she said,
Had lovingly made leather trousers.
Costly-weft, yellow-mottled cloth of Bukhara—
With that yellow-mottled cloth she lined them.
My poor mother Kanykei,
For many days and many nights,
Worked the stitching without rest.
Why, when those trousers were pulled,
They stretched like sinew;
When those trousers were released,
They drew back like glue.
In places all over those trousers,
She set in piping that dazzled the eye.
A whole otter pelt
She had slit apart,
And set round the trouser cuffs.
Those most wondrous leather trousers
They put upon Kulchoro.
At the bottom of that saddlebag,
Your dignified mother Kanykei,
‘He will know this service of mine,’ she said,
‘Kulchoro, left behind by Almam,
Will wear it as my entrusted gift,’ she said.
Crafted with consummate skill,
A costly gray lynx-fur cap
My grieving mother Kanykei
Had made for Kulchoro.
Acknowledging his orphanhood,
That cap his mother had made
They put upon Kulchoro.
Rekindling his extinguished fire,
Almambet's orphan's
Dead soul they revived.
To Burulcha and Kulchoro's,
The two sorrowful ones' house,
They had a pale-gray mare caught and brought,
And dedicated it to Almambet,
Having the pale-gray mare slaughtered.
They cut off chunks of yellow butter.
They began a special undertaking:
A weaned lamb, a savory head,
In the widow and orphan's house
They set boiling furiously.
Let us leave this here,
And begin from this side.
With heroic Bakai accompanying him,
This orphan, Manas's son, said:
“If my appointed death comes, I shall die.
Abyke, Kobosh, my six elder kinsmen—
I shall go and greet them.
If my elder kinsmen are good,
The inheritance left by my father,
My kin who will turn toward me,
The Buurul horse left by the Generous One,
The swift steed left by my father—
I shall go and ask them face to face.
If the saint grants this undertaking,
I shall look to his blessing.
My six exceptionally powerful elder kinsmen,
I shall take as my elder brothers.
A khan equal to my father,
My elder kinsman Abyke is there.
I shall agree to what he says;
I shall give him my mother Kanykei in marriage.
This year, driving seventy red nar camels,
If I do not braid each tail,
My six elder kinsmen like Ala-Too,
If I do not give these as tribute—
I have languished for many years;
If I do not see their faces this year,
Loading gold by the pood,
If I do not give it as a first-sighting gift,
If I do not see their faces this year,
To my kindly uncle Abyke,
If I do not offer my mother Kanykei,
If I do not prosper, settling beside them,
If I do not return and settle in Talas this year,
If I do not prosper among my kin this year—
Fighting the enemy together,
Pressing our claims together,
My valiant kinsman Abyke,
If I do not bind him as my support,
From Beijing's people, from Kakan,
If I do not boldly seek the blood-price,
This year, putting our knowledge together,
Uniting in this way,
Upon the swarming unbelievers,
If I do not launch a mighty holy war,
There is so much vengeance for my father—
If I do not wreak slaughter upon the Chinese!
Uncle Bakai, hear my words.
Taking the six as my support,
If I do not gather khojas and mullahs,
Gathering lions,
Peers equal to myself,
If my six elder kinsmen agree with my way,
The Argyn and the Kyrgyz,
If I do not gather them in great numbers,
Bringing them all,
If I do not set them marching in a long line—
When a black musket cracks,
From warriors who will not flee,
When a fierce musket snaps,
From champions who will not start,
From those skilled and deft with the spear,
From the strongest wielders of the battle-axe,
From warriors who charge armies,
From marksmen who shoot the eye,
Who plunge into thick dust,
When a great battle truly comes,
When they meet a mighty enemy,
Who stand and fight without fleeing,
If I do not gather a mighty army—
If my six elder kinsmen support me,
Against the Kara Kalmyks and Torguts,
If I do not wreak devastation,
This year, upon those damned Chinese,
If I do not inflict a mighty slaughter!
Along Uch-Koshoi,
Shygai's son Chynkozho,
If I do not bind him as my support,
Bakai's son Baitailak,
Sary Khan's Kalyk,
Zhamgyrchy's Shaiymbet,
Tekeche's Ormonbek—
All sons of khans,
If I do not gather every one without exception,
If my six elder kinsmen do not despise me,
This year, spreading a boundless army,
The red banner with a golden crescent,
Putting it in Khan Bakai's hands,
Upon the Chinese of Beijing ahead,
If I do not inflict a mighty slaughter!
If my kin do not turn aside,
If I do not wreak havoc upon the Chinese,
Among the people of Chynmachyn,
Famed throughout the world,
From their giant Khan Kongurbai,
From all the countless Chinese,
If I do not charge and make war,
If my kin follow without objection,
Upon the Kara Chinese and Manchus,
If I do not avenge the khans!
Distant Beijing, looming dark—
There is vengeance for my forefather's death.
If I do not enter straight and wage war,
If my kin stand firm,
Upon the grim Chinese and Kalmyks,
If I do not enter straight and take revenge,
Grasping a spear, breaking their ranks,
Fighting until I fall to a bullet!”
This undertaking he spoke of
Was Semetey's desire.
What was unknown is revealed by
Your uncle Khan Bakai's anxious thoughts.
Your uncle Bakai said this;
Listen—he speaks of terrible things:
“While Abyke and Kobosh are there,
My beloved only one,
While your six elder kinsmen live,
This Talas is no land for you;
These Kyrgyz are no people for you.
While your six elder kinsmen remain alive,
While vile Kobosh commits his folly,
This Keng-Kol is no land for you;
These Argyn are no people for you.
Let me tell you of your elder Abyke:
He was a kindhearted kinsman and hero.
If you ask about Kobosh,
He was a deeply ignorant dog;
What man was he, if not a dog?
Because of that swine,
We lived lost and wandering;
We saw pitch-dark nights;
We saw devastation.
When dog Kobosh inflicted humiliation,
When he plundered the palace,
Into Temirkan's city
We wandered and made a life.
Fearing someone with a grudge would slaughter you,
